s01_hook: [curious] Quick question. What's the very first thing you remember? [short pause] Got it? Okay. [lowers voice, mysterious] Here's the weird part. Whatever it is, you were probably at least three years old. [amazed] That means more than a thousand days of your life, the days you learned to walk, to talk, to recognize your mom's face, are just... [whispering] gone. [dramatic] Deleted. [curious] So where did they go?
s02_title: [excited] Why can't you remember being a baby?
s03_babies: [confident] First, let's kill a myth. Babies are not bad at remembering. [storytelling] In the nineteen eighties, a scientist named Carolyn Rovee-Collier tied a ribbon from a baby's ankle to a mobile hanging over the crib. [playful] Kick, and the mobile moves. [laughs softly] Babies figured that out fast. [impressed] And when she brought them back a week later, three-month-olds still remembered, and started kicking right away. Older babies remembered for months. [excited] So babies do make memories. Tons of them. [serious] The problem is, they don't last.
s04_name: [intrigued] Scientists have a name for this. [slowly] Infantile amnesia. [dramatic] And there are three big suspects.
s05_hippo: [detective voice] Suspect number one: your brain was a construction site. [curious] Deep inside your brain is a part shaped a bit like a seahorse, called the hippocampus. Its job is to take what happens to you and save it as a memory. [serious] But in babies, the hippocampus is still being built. It keeps making brand-new neurons, and every new neuron that wires in can scramble the connections that were already there. [frustrated] Imagine writing in a notebook while someone keeps adding and ripping out pages. [impressed] In experiments with baby mice, when scientists slowed down that new-neuron growth, the mice forgot less.
s06_words: [detective voice] Suspect number two: you had no words. [casual] Grown-up memories are like files with labels. [happy] My tenth birthday. [wincing] The day I broke my arm. [gentle] But a baby has no words to label anything. So even if the memory is in there, later, when you think in words, you can't search for it. [playful] It's like a file saved in a format your computer can't open anymore.
s07_me: [detective voice] Suspect number three: there was no you yet. [thoughtful] To remember something happening to you, you need a sense of me. Most babies don't recognize themselves in a mirror until around eighteen months. [softly] Before that, there's no main character to build the story around.
s08_seven: [excited] Now here's what's really strange. Little kids actually remember their baby years for a while. [storytelling] Psychologist Patricia Bauer recorded three-year-olds talking with their moms about things they'd done. Years later, she checked what they still remembered. At five, six and seven, the kids remembered most of it. [surprised] By eight and nine, only about a third. [serious] So the big forgetting doesn't happen when you're a baby. [dramatic] It happens around age seven.
s09_locked: [mysterious] But wait. Are those memories really deleted? [whispering] Maybe not. [excited] In twenty eighteen, researchers in Toronto gave baby mice a memory, waited until they had forgotten it, and then used light to switch on the exact brain cells that stored it. [amazed] And the mice remembered. The memory was still there. [softly] They just couldn't find the door. [excited] And in twenty twenty-five, a team at Yale scanned babies' brains, and saw the hippocampus saving new memories from about one year old. [whispering] So your baby memories might be locked away inside you, right now.
s10_fake: [curious] Which brings us back to your first memory. In a survey of more than six thousand people, almost forty percent said they remembered something from age two or younger. [skeptical] Scientists think most of those are fake. [reassuring] Not lies. Your brain stitched them together from photos, family stories and things you were told, and then filed them as real.
s11_end: [warm] So, why can't you remember being a baby? Your brain was under construction, you had no words, and no me. And around age seven, your brain cleaned house. [heartfelt] But the baby you were didn't disappear. Every word you know, every face you trust, every step you take, you learned in the years you forgot. [playful] So, what's your earliest memory? Drop it in the comments, [laughs] and I'll tell you if it's fake.
